fangen.et:
From Middle High German vāhen, from Old High German fāhan, a strong verb with past forms fieng, gefangan, from Proto-West Germanic *fą̄han, from Proto-Germanic *fanhaną.
The present stem fang- is derived from the past forms. This development spread from Middle…

fancy.et: Borrowed from English fancy. Doublet of Fantasie.

Fan.et: Borrowed from English fan, short for fanatic.

Fang.et: From Middle High German vanc, ultimately from the root of fangen (“to catch”).

s: fang (long animal tooth used for tearing flesh)

fantastisch.et: From Latin phantasticus, with assimilation to native suffix -isch. By surface analysis, Fantast (“fantasist, dreamer”) + -isch.

fanatisch.et: Borrowed from French fanatique, from Latin fānāticus.

Fantasie.et: From Middle High German fantasīe (whence also the obsolete doublet Phantasei), learned borrowing from Latin phantasia, from Ancient Greek φᾰντᾰσῐ́ᾱ (phăntăsĭ́ā). Doublet of fancy and Fantasia.
